notes:
1. Employment — Meaning and Development Importance

  • Employment means participation in productive economic activity for wages, salary, profit, family gain or another economic return.
  • Employment supports household income, poverty reduction, skill development, production, tax revenue, dignity and social participation.
  • Employment policy must examine not only the number of jobs but also their productivity, wages, security and social protection.
📌 Must-Memorise

Employment Quality → Jobs + Productivity + Wages + Security + Social Protection

2. Employment Generation vs Employment Conditions

  • Chapter 14 focused on how employment is generated through agriculture, industry, services, MSMEs, infrastructure and entrepreneurship.
  • This chapter focuses on:
  • Labour-market measurement.
  • Employment composition.
  • Unemployment.
  • Underemployment.
  • Wages.
  • Labour rights.
  • Social security.
  • Worker protection.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Employment Generation ≠ Employment Measurement and Labour Conditions

3. Labour Force

  • Labour force broadly consists of employed persons plus unemployed persons who satisfy the applicable criteria of seeking or being available for work.
📌 Must-Memorise

Labour Force = Employed + Unemployed

4. Workforce

  • Workforce consists only of persons who are actually employed.
📌 Must-Memorise

Workforce = Employed Persons

5. Labour Force vs Workforce

  • Labour force → Employed + unemployed.
  • Workforce → Employed only.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Labour Force ≠ Workforce

6. Persons Outside the Labour Force

Depending on their activity status, persons outside the labour force can include:

  • Students.
  • Homemakers.
  • Elderly persons.
  • Others neither working nor seeking/available for work.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Outside Labour Force ≠ Automatically Unemployed

7. Labour Force Participation Rate — LFPR

  • LFPR stands for Labour Force Participation Rate.
  • It measures the proportion of the relevant population that is in the labour force.
📌 Must-Memorise

LFPR = Labour Force ÷ Population × 100

8. Worker Population Ratio — WPR

  • WPR stands for Worker Population Ratio.
  • It measures the proportion of the relevant population that is employed.
📌 Must-Memorise

WPR = Workers ÷ Population × 100

9. Unemployment Rate — UR

  • UR stands for Unemployment Rate.
  • It measures unemployed persons as a percentage of the labour force.
📌 Must-Memorise

UR = Unemployed Persons ÷ Labour Force × 100

10. LFPR, WPR and UR — Core Difference

  • LFPR → Labour-market participation.
  • WPR → Actual employment.
  • UR → Unemployment within the labour force.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

UR Denominator → Labour Force, Not Total Population

11. PLFS — Periodic Labour Force Survey

  • PLFS stands for Periodic Labour Force Survey.
  • It is conducted by the National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
  • It estimates major indicators such as LFPR, WPR and unemployment.
📌 Must-Memorise

PLFS → Official Labour-Market Survey

12. Usual Status

  • Usual Status examines a person's activity over a relatively longer reference period.
  • The expression ps + ss means Principal Status + Subsidiary Status.
📌 Must-Memorise

ps + ss → Principal Status + Subsidiary Status

13. Current Weekly Status — CWS

  • CWS stands for Current Weekly Status.
  • It uses the preceding seven-day reference period.
📌 Must-Memorise

CWS → Previous 7 Days

14. Usual Status vs CWS

  • Usual Status → Longer reference period.
  • CWS → Seven-day reference period.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Different Reference Periods Can Produce Different Employment Estimates

  • LFPR → 59.3%.
  • WPR → 57.4%.
  • Unemployment Rate → 3.1%.

16. PLFS 2025 — Male and Female LFPR

According to the supplied source:

  • Female LFPR → 40.0%.
📌 Must-Memorise

17. PLFS 2025 — Absolute Employment Estimate

  • The supplied source states that approximately 61.6 crore persons aged 15+ were employed on average during 2025 using projected population figures for generating the absolute estimate.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Absolute PLFS Estimate ≠ Census Count

18. Employment Statistics — Always Check the Basis

Employment figures can vary according to:

  • Age group.
  • Rural/urban location.
  • Gender.
  • Reference period.
  • Usual Status or CWS.
📌 Must-Memorise

Never Quote an Unemployment Number Without Its Statistical Basis

19. Three Broad Employment Statuses

PLFS broadly classifies workers into:

  • Self-employed.
  • Regular wage/salaried.
  • Casual labour.

20. Self-Employment

Self-employment can include:

  • Own-account workers.
  • Employers.
  • Specified helpers in household enterprises.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Self-Employment ≠ Always Entrepreneurship

21. Regular Wage or Salaried Employment

  • A regular wage or salaried worker receives wages or salary on a relatively regular basis from an employer.
  • Such employment may provide greater income stability than casual work, though conditions vary.

22. Casual Labour

  • Casual workers are generally employed on an occasional or short-duration basis and paid according to work performed.

Common sectors include:

  • Agriculture.
  • Construction.
  • Loading and unloading.
  • Other labour-intensive work.

23. PLFS 2025 — Employment Status Composition

According to the supplied source:

  • Self-employed → 56.2%.
  • Regular wage/salaried → 23.6%.
  • Casual labour → About 20.2%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Largest Employment Status in PLFS 2025 → Self-Employment

24. Open Unemployment

  • Open unemployment occurs when a person willing and able to work is unable to obtain employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Open Unemployment → No Job

25. Seasonal Unemployment

  • Seasonal unemployment arises when jobs are available only during certain periods of the year.
  • It is especially associated with activities such as agriculture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Seasonal Unemployment → Work Available Only in Certain Seasons

26. Disguised Unemployment

  • Disguised unemployment occurs when more workers are engaged than are required.
  • Removing some workers may not significantly reduce total output.
  • It is commonly associated with traditional agriculture and small family enterprises.
📌 Must-Memorise

Disguised Unemployment → Excess Workers

27. Structural Unemployment

  • Structural unemployment arises when worker skills, occupations or locations do not match available jobs.
  • Technological and industrial change can contribute to it.
📌 Must-Memorise

Structural Unemployment → Labour-Market Mismatch

28. Frictional Unemployment

  • Frictional unemployment is temporary unemployment during movement between jobs or while entering the labour market and searching for work.

29. Cyclical Unemployment

  • Cyclical unemployment is associated with economic downturns that reduce demand, production and employment.

30. Technological Unemployment

  • Technological unemployment can arise when automation, machinery or software reduces demand for certain kinds of labour.
  • Technology can simultaneously eliminate some jobs and create new occupations.

31. Educated Unemployment

Educated unemployment can arise from:

  • Skill mismatch.
  • Insufficient suitable jobs.
  • Geographic mismatch.
  • Occupational expectations.
  • Weak education-industry linkage.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Education ≠ Automatic Employment

32. Underemployment

  • Underemployment occurs when a person is employed but labour is not fully utilised in terms of:
  • Working time.
  • Skills.
  • Productivity.
  • Income potential.
📌 Must-Memorise

Underemployment → Working, But Underutilised

33. Time-Related and Skill Underemployment

  • Time-related underemployment → Worker gets fewer hours than desired.
  • Skill underutilisation → Worker has substantially higher skills than the job requires.

34. Unemployment vs Underemployment vs Disguised Unemployment

  • Unemployment → No qualifying employment.
  • Underemployment → Working, but labour is underused.
  • Disguised unemployment → Some apparent workers add little or no extra output.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

These Three Concepts Are Different

35. Marginal Productivity and Disguised Unemployment

  • In disguised unemployment, some workers may have very low or near-zero marginal productivity.
  • Moving them into productive non-farm work may raise overall output without significantly reducing farm production.

36. Sectoral Employment — Structural Transformation

Long-term development generally involves movement from:

Low-Productivity Agriculture

→ Manufacturing + Construction + Modern Services

→ Higher-Productivity Employment

37. Agriculture — Employment Share

According to PLFS 2025 in the supplied source:

  • Agriculture accounted for 43.0% of employment.
  • It had declined from 44.8% in 2024.
📌 Must-Memorise

PLFS 2025 Agriculture Employment Share → 43.0%

38. Manufacturing and Construction — Employment Share

According to the supplied PLFS 2025 figures:

  • Manufacturing → 12.1%.
  • Construction → About 12.0%.

39. Agriculture — Employment-Output Imbalance

  • Agriculture employs a much larger share of workers than its relative contribution to output.
  • This indicates significant productivity differences between sectors.

40. Manufacturing and Construction — Employment Role

Manufacturing:

  • Can absorb workers leaving agriculture.
  • Can create supply-chain employment.

Construction:

  • Is a major source of casual and migrant employment.
  • Can absorb workers at varying skill levels.

41. Services — Diverse Employment Structure

Services include both lower- and higher-productivity work.

Examples range from:

  • Retail.
  • Transport.
  • Hospitality.

to:

  • IT.
  • Finance.
  • Professional services.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Service-Sector Employment ≠ Always High-Productivity Employment

42. Organised Sector

  • The organised sector generally includes establishments operating within formal regulatory and institutional frameworks.
  • Workers are more likely to have contracts, regular wages and social security, but this is not automatic.

43. Unorganised Sector

Examples include:

  • Street vendors.
  • Domestic workers.
  • Small farmers.
  • Construction workers.
  • Home-based workers.
  • Small workshop workers.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Unorganised Worker ≠ Unemployed Worker

44. Formal Employment

  • Formal employment generally involves employment relationships covered by formal rules, contracts and social-security arrangements.

45. Informal Employment

  • Informal employment can exist even inside an organised enterprise when workers lack formal protection or social-security benefits.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Organised Sector ≠ Every Worker Formally Employed

46. Youth Unemployment

According to PLFS 2025 in the supplied source, for persons aged 15–29 under Usual Status:

  • Overall youth unemployment → 9.9%.
  • Rural youth unemployment → 8.3%.
  • Urban youth unemployment → 13.6%.
📌 Must-Memorise

PLFS 2025 Youth UR → 9.9%

47. Why Youth Unemployment Can Be High

Young workers may face:

  • Lack of experience.
  • Skill mismatch.
  • Competition for formal jobs.
  • Geographic mismatch.
  • Long job-search periods.
  • Occupational expectations.

48. Educated Unemployment — PLFS 2025

  • The supplied source states that unemployment among persons aged 15+ with secondary education and above was 6.5% under Usual Status in PLFS 2025.
📌 Must-Memorise

Higher Education ≠ Guaranteed Job

49. NEET

  • NEET means Not in Employment, Education or Training.
  • PLFS 2025 in the supplied source estimated 25.0% of persons aged 15–29 in the NEET category.
📌 Must-Memorise

NEET → Not in Employment, Education or Training

50. Youth Unemployment vs NEET

  • Youth unemployment → Young people satisfying labour-force unemployment criteria.
  • NEET → Broader group not in employment, education or training.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

NEET ≠ Unemployment Rate

51. Women's Labour-Force Participation

According to PLFS 2025 for persons aged 15+ under Usual Status:

  • Female LFPR → 40.0%.
  • Female WPR → 38.8%.
  • Male LFPR → 79.1%.
  • Male WPR → 76.6%.

52. Barriers to Women's Employment

Important barriers include:

  • Unpaid care responsibilities.
  • Childcare.
  • Safety.
  • Transport.
  • Social norms.
  • Workplace discrimination.
  • Occupational segregation.
  • Availability of suitable jobs.

53. Unpaid Care Work

  • Women perform substantial unpaid household and care work.
  • Such activity may not be counted as employment where it does not satisfy the prescribed economic-activity definition.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Economically Valuable Unpaid Care ≠ Necessarily Counted as Employment

54. Women's Employment — Development Importance

Greater women's productive employment can:

  • Raise household income.
  • Expand labour supply.
  • Increase economic independence.
  • Strengthen human capital.
  • Support economic growth.

55. Employment Quality and Decent Work

Job quality depends on:

  • Adequate wages.
  • Income stability.
  • Safe working conditions.
  • Reasonable working hours.
  • Social security.
  • Protection from discrimination.
  • Skill development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Having a Job ≠ Necessarily Having a Good Job

56. Nominal Wage vs Real Wage

  • Nominal wage → Money amount received.
  • Real wage → Purchasing power of that money after accounting for prices.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Nominal Wage Increase ≠ Real Wage Increase

57. Minimum Wage

  • A minimum wage is the legally prescribed wage floor for covered employment under the applicable labour-law framework.
  • The supplied source identifies the Code on Wages, 2019 as the principal central statutory framework after implementation of the Labour Codes.

58. Productivity and Wages

Productivity can rise through:

  • Skills.
  • Technology.
  • Better management.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Capital investment.
  • Higher productivity can support wage growth.
  • But productivity gains do not automatically guarantee proportional wage increases for every worker.

59. Four Labour Codes

India consolidated 29 Central labour laws into four Labour Codes:

1. Code on Wages, 2019.

2. Industrial Relations Code, 2020.

3. Code on Social Security, 2020.

4. Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.

📌 Must-Memorise

29 Central Labour Laws → 4 Labour Codes

60. Labour Codes — Effective Date in Supplied Source

According to the supplied source:

  • The four Labour Codes became effective from 21 November 2025.
📌 Must-Memorise

4 Labour Codes → Effective 21 November 2025

⚠️ TNPSC Current-Affairs Note

Older notes stating that the Labour Codes were enacted but not implemented are outdated according to the supplied 2026 source.

61. Code on Wages — 2019

The Code on Wages consolidates central legislation concerning:

  • Minimum wages.
  • Payment of wages.
  • Bonus.
  • Equal-remuneration principles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Code on Wages → 2019

62. Industrial Relations Code — 2020

The Industrial Relations Code deals with:

  • Trade unions.
  • Industrial disputes.
  • Standing orders.
  • Industrial relations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Relations Code → 2020

63. Code on Social Security — 2020

The Code on Social Security provides a consolidated framework covering areas such as:

  • Provident fund.
  • Employee insurance.
  • Gratuity.
  • Other social-security protections.
  • Gig workers.
  • Platform workers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Code on Social Security → 2020

64. Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code — 2020

  • The OSHWC Code consolidates 13 Central labour laws relating to occupational safety, health and working conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

OSHWC Code → 2020 → Safety + Health + Working Conditions

65. Four Labour Codes — Memory Chain

  • Wages → Code on Wages.
  • Unions and disputes → Industrial Relations Code.
  • Benefits and worker protection → Social Security Code.
  • Safety and working conditions → OSHWC Code.

66. Social Security — Meaning

Social security protects workers against economic risks such as:

  • Old age.
  • Disability.
  • Illness.
  • Maternity.
  • Employment injury.
  • Loss of earning capacity.

67. EPFO and ESIC

  • EPFO → Provident-fund and pension-oriented social-security institution for covered employees.
  • ESIC → Employee social-insurance and medical-benefit institution for covered workers.
📌 Must-Memorise

EPFO → Provident Fund

ESIC → Social Insurance + Medical Benefits

68. e-Shram

  • e-Shram is maintained by the Ministry of Labour and Employment as a national database of unorganised workers.
  • It supports registration and linkage with welfare and social-security programmes.

It can include workers such as:

  • Domestic workers.
  • Construction workers.
  • Street vendors.
  • Agricultural workers.
  • Other eligible unorganised workers.
📌 Must-Memorise

e-Shram → National Database of Unorganised Workers

69. e-Shram vs EPFO vs ESIC

  • e-Shram → Unorganised-worker database and welfare linkage.
  • EPFO → Provident fund and pension.
  • ESIC → Employee social insurance and medical benefits.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

e-Shram ≠ Employment-Guarantee Scheme

70. Gig Economy

  • Gig work is organised around short-term tasks, assignments or contractual arrangements rather than only traditional long-term employment.

Possible examples include:

  • Ride services.
  • Delivery.
  • Logistics.
  • Freelance digital work.
  • Home-service work.

71. Platform Work

  • Platform work is a type of gig work in which a digital platform connects workers with customers or clients.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Gig Work ≠ Platform Work in Every Case

Platform Work ⊂ Gig Work

72. Gig Work — Benefits and Challenges

Potential benefits:

  • Flexible entry.
  • Flexible schedules.
  • Additional income.
  • Digital opportunities.

Challenges:

  • Irregular income.
  • Limited security.
  • Algorithmic control.
  • Occupational risk.
  • Weak traditional benefits.
  • Representation difficulties.

73. Gig and Platform Workers — Social Security

  • The supplied source notes that the Code on Social Security, 2020 expressly includes gig workers and platform workers within its social-security framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gig + Platform Workers → Social Security Code, 2020

74. Employment and Migration

Employment can drive:

  • Rural–urban migration.
  • Rural–rural migration.
  • Urban–urban migration.
  • Inter-district migration.
  • Inter-State migration.
  • International migration.

75. Migrant Workers — Push and Pull Factors

Push factors include:

  • Low wages.
  • Agricultural distress.
  • Seasonal employment.
  • Lack of jobs.
  • Disasters.

Pull factors include:

  • Higher wages.
  • Industrial employment.
  • Construction jobs.
  • Service employment.
  • Better career opportunities.

76. Migrant-Worker Challenges

Migrant workers may face:

  • Insecure housing.
  • Irregular employment.
  • Weak support networks.
  • Social-security portability issues.
  • Language barriers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Migration Policy → Employment + Portability + Worker Protection

77. National Career Service — NCS

  • NCS stands for National Career Service.
  • It was launched on 20 July 2015 as a Mission Mode Project under the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

NCS → 20 July 2015

78. National Career Service — Functions

NCS provides:

  • Job-search services.
  • Employer registration.
  • Career counselling.
  • Job fairs.
  • Career centres.
  • Employment information.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

NCS Facilitates Employment

NCS Does Not Guarantee a Job

79. Employment Exchanges

Employment Exchanges traditionally perform functions such as:

  • Job-seeker registration.
  • Vacancy notification under applicable frameworks.
  • Employment information.
  • Vocational guidance.
  • Many such functions are increasingly integrated with digital platforms.

80. Employability

Employability means the ability to obtain and perform productive employment.

It depends on:

  • Technical skills.
  • Communication.
  • Digital literacy.
  • Problem-solving.
  • Work experience.
  • Adaptability.
  • Occupational knowledge.

81. Skill Mismatch

Skill mismatch may involve:

  • Too few skills.
  • Outdated skills.
  • Skills in weak-demand fields.
  • Qualifications higher than the available job requires.
📌 Must-Memorise

Skill Mismatch → Worker Capability ≠ Job Requirement

82. Information Mismatch vs Capability Mismatch

  • Information mismatch → Job seekers and employers cannot find one another efficiently.
  • Capability mismatch → Workers do not possess skills required by available jobs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Career Portals → Reduce Information Mismatch

Skill Training → Reduce Capability Mismatch

  • Persons aged 15–29 → 5.0%.
  • These figures highlight the importance of expanding practical and industry-aligned training.

📌 Must-Memorise

Private Jobs Portal → Job Matching

87. TNSDC

  • TNSDC stands for Tamil Nadu Skill Development Corporation.
  • It supports job-oriented skill-development programmes for youth.

88. Tamil Nadu — Career Guidance and Unemployment Assistance

  • Tamil Nadu provides career-guidance services for youth.
  • The State also maintains an unemployment-assistance framework for eligible employment registrants.
  • Eligibility and assistance amounts can change and should be treated as current scheme details.

89. Tamil Nadu — Major Employment Challenges

Important issues include:

  • Youth unemployment.
  • Educated unemployment.
  • Skill mismatch.
  • Informal employment.
  • Migrant-worker welfare.
  • Women's employment.
  • Transition towards technology-intensive industry.

90. Employment Policy — Final Objective

Employment policy should move from:

Any Job

towards:

Productive

  • Secure
  • Skilled
  • Adequately Paid
  • Socially Protected Employment

98. TNPSC Traps

  • Labour force and workforce are different.
  • Labour force includes employed and unemployed persons satisfying applicable criteria.
  • Workforce includes employed persons only.
  • LFPR and WPR use population as the denominator.
  • UR uses labour force as the denominator.
  • A student or homemaker outside the labour force is not automatically unemployed.
  • PLFS and Census are different.
  • Usual Status and CWS are different.
  • CWS uses a seven-day reference period.
  • Low unemployment does not prove high employment quality.
  • Open unemployment and disguised unemployment are different.
  • Underemployment and unemployment are different.
  • Disguised unemployment involves very low or near-zero marginal productivity for some workers.
  • Structural unemployment involves mismatch.
  • Frictional unemployment can occur even in a healthy economy.
  • Self-employment is not always high-quality entrepreneurship.
  • Regular salaried and casual employment are different.
  • Organised sector and formal employment are not exact synonyms.
  • Unorganised worker does not mean unemployed worker.
  • Youth unemployment and educated unemployment are different.
  • NEET is broader than unemployment.
  • Nominal and real wages are different.
  • Agriculture still had the largest employment share in the supplied PLFS 2025 data.
  • Higher industrial output does not automatically guarantee high employment.
  • Four Labour Codes consolidated 29 Central labour laws.
  • According to the supplied source, the four Labour Codes became effective on 21 November 2025.
  • Code on Wages → 2019.
  • Industrial Relations Code → 2020.
  • Social Security Code → 2020.
  • OSHWC Code → 2020.
  • e-Shram is a database and welfare-linkage platform, not an employment guarantee.
  • EPFO, ESIC and e-Shram are different.
  • Gig work and platform work are related but not identical.
  • MGNREGA guarantees qualifying rural wage employment; NCS does not.
  • NCS is an employment and career-service platform.
  • NCS launched → 20 July 2015.
  • TNSDC focuses on skill development.
  • Tamil Nadu Private Jobs Portal focuses on job matching.
  • Employment generation was covered separately in Chapter 14.
